dossier.public_summary: The dip repeats every 0.825 days and has a second eclipse half an orbit later that is almost as deep as the first, indicating two stars eclipsing each other. The out-of-eclipse light also pulsates strongly and the dip depth shifts by hundreds of percent, matching the star's 0.412-day spin. Together this is an eclipsing M-dwarf binary folded to the 0.825-day period, not a planet.

reasons.why: A second dip at half-phase at ~47% of the primary dip depth is stellar occultation depth, far too deep for a hot-Jupiter occultation. Its depth is half the transit depth and its SNR is well above the best brightening, proving the 0.825 d signal is an eclipsing binary at twice the period (1.65 d), folded with odd and even eclipses.

reasons.why: Large out-of-eclipse swing at this period, larger than the dip itself with very high chi2, is typical of spots/ellipsoidal variation from a close binary, not a planet.

Depth changes dramatically within the same pipeline (e.g., sector 52 6112 ppm vs sector 84 216 ppm), inconsistent with a stable planetary transit and expected when a spotty active M-dwarf binaries eclipse are folded with its rotation.

Dip period is exactly twice the measured stellar rotation period with huge spot variability; strong phase curve plus secondary supports a tidally locked active M-dwarf eclipsing binary rather than a coincidental planetary period.
Long duration and density mismatch (fit_log_density_ratio=-2.067, star_density_penalty=4165) plus large secondary favour a small-star eclipse diluted to ~2100 ppm over a planet around this M-dwarf.
